strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical bottleneck in state-of-the-art biomolecular structure prediction (AlphaFold3/Boltz-1 style models): the heavy computational and memory footprint of the Pairformer backbone.

Strong and convincing empirical results: Pairmixer matches the performance of the full Pairformer backbone across protein folding and docking benchmarks while achieving up to 4x faster inference on long sequences and reducing training cost by 34%.

Concrete downstream validation: The authors integrated Pairmixer into a binder design pipeline (BindFast), demonstrating that it can handle 30% larger target proteins without running out of memory (OOM) and yields over 2x faster sampling.

The analytical experiments are excellent. The use of the Match3 toy task and the low-norm dropout inference sparsification provide valuable conceptual insights into how triangle multiplication models sparse higher-order interactions without needing full triangle attention.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, clear, and includes comprehensive training and evaluation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: While Pairmixer matches the baseline on most metrics, there is a noticeable performance drop in protein-protein docking (DockQ) on CASP15 (e.g., 0.52 vs 0.64 for Large Phase 2). This suggest that removing sequence updates and triangle attention might slightly affect the model's ability to resolve complex multimeric interfaces.

By completely removing sequence updates from the backbone ($s^{backbone} = s^{init}$), the sequence representation remains static throughout the backbone blocks. This design effectively offloads all sequence-pair co-evolution and co-refinement reasoning to the diffusion module.

The model lacks a trained confidence model, meaning 'top-1' performance is reported using the first prediction. While the oracle (best-of-5) results provide a fair comparison, having a trained confidence model would make the system more complete for real-world deployment.

strengths: Significant computational efficiency gains: The proposed Pairmixer architecture eliminates triangle attention and sequence updates in the backbone, achieving up to 4x faster inference on long sequences and reducing training costs by 34% in GPU-days.

Thorough and high-quality evaluation: The authors retrain Boltz-1 level large models from scratch and test them across small, medium, and large scales on established benchmarks (RCSB, CASP15), showing that Pairmixer achieves comparable accuracy to the full Pairformer.

Practical downstream utility: The paper demonstrates the real-world value of the proposed architecture by integrating it into a binder design framework (BindFast), leading to 2x-2.6x speedups and enabling design on 30% longer target sequences without running out of memory (OOM).

Deep analytical insights: The manuscript provides compelling analyses of why triangle multiplication is sufficient, including low-norm vs. random dropout at inference to highlight its sparsity-capturing behavior, and the synthetic Match3 task to demonstrate representation capacity.

Excellent clarity and presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly informative figures, detailed FLOPs calculations in the appendix, and clear schematics of the architectures.
weaknesses: Minor performance trade-offs: There are some performance drops in specific cofolding metrics, such as a decrease in DockQ on the CASP15 dataset (from 0.64 down to 0.52 in Large Phase 2) compared to the full Pairformer backbone.

Lack of a trained confidence model: Since a confidence model was not trained for Pairmixer, the top-1 predictions are reported using the first sample instead of a ranked selection, which makes the direct comparison of top-1 performance with baseline systems less optimal.

strengths: Significant efficiency and speed improvements (up to 4x faster inference on long sequences, 34% reduction in training GPU-days) on a highly relevant and computationally bottlenecked task (AlphaFold3-style biomolecular co-folding).

Rigorous scale-up evaluation, training multiple model sizes (Small, Medium, Large) from scratch and benchmarking on diverse modalities (protein folding, protein-protein docking, and protein-ligand docking) using RCSB and CASP15 test sets.

Strong real-world validation via integration into a downstream binder design pipeline (BoltzDesign / BindFast), demonstrating over 2x faster sampling and a 30% increase in sequence length limits without running out of memory (OOM).

Thoughtful and deep empirical analyses, such as the inference-time sparsification/dropout experiments and representation learning evaluation on the synthetic Match3 task, which provide concrete mechanistic insights into why triangle multiplication works so well.
Excellent presentation, clear figures, and high transparency with detailed hyperparameter tables and FLOPs breakdown in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core architectural components (triangle multiplication and feed-forward networks) are not novel on their own, as they were introduced in AlphaFold2. The primary novelty is the empirical demonstration that triangle attention and sequence updates can be fully omitted in the backbone.

There is a noticeable performance regression in protein-protein docking quality (DockQ score), especially visible on the CASP15 dataset (dropping from 0.64 to 0.52 in the large model). While CASP15 has a small sample size (n=14), this suggests that removing triangle attention might slightly compromise the model's ability to capture complex multimeric interfaces.

The current implementation does not train a confidence model (e.g., predicting pLDDT or PAE/confidence scores), which is a critical feature for real-world biologist workflows to filter out low-confidence structural predictions.

The transition of MSA processing is slightly ambiguous; more explicit clarification on whether any forms of attention remain inside the shallow MSA module would benefit the reproducibility of the backbone simplification.

strengths: High Practical Impact: The paper introduces Pairmixer, a highly efficient alternative to the Pairformer backbone of AlphaFold3/Boltz-1, achieving up to 4x faster inference on long sequences and reducing training cost by 34% while maintaining structural accuracy.

Comprehensive Evaluation: The authors evaluate the model across a wide range of biomolecular cofolding modalities (protein-protein, protein-ligand, antibody-antigen, protein-nucleic acid, and RNA structures) on standard benchmarks like RCSB and CASP15.

Validation on Downstream Applications: The authors integrated Pairmixer into BoltzDesign (resulting in BindFast), demonstrating over 2x speedups in binder design and the ability to scale to ~30% larger protein complexes without running out of memory (OOM).

Deep Architectural Analysis: The paper goes beyond simple performance tables by including insightful analyses, such as testing on the synthetic Match3 task to demonstrate the mathematical expressivity of triangle multiplication, and evaluating model robustness under sparse/low-norm dropouts.
weaknesses: Incremental Architectural Novelty: The primary method is a simplification of the existing AlphaFold3/Pairformer architecture (by removing sequence updates and triangle attention, leaving only triangle multiplication). While the reduction is highly effective and well-demonstrated, the individual components themselves are not newly designed.

Dependence on the Diffusion Module: In cofolding models like Boltz-1, the trunk (backbone) outputs are processed by a multi-layer transformer-based diffusion module. It remains slightly unclear to what extent the attention layers within the diffusion module compensate for the sequence attention removed from the trunk backbone.

Comparisons to Other Simplified Baselines: While the authors compare Pairmixer against standard sequence-only Transformers, a direct empirical comparison with other recent simplified protein folding backbones (e.g., SimpleFold, MiniFold) would further strengthen the positioning of this work.

strengths: Outstanding Efficiency Improvements: Pairmixer delivers up to 4x faster inference on long sequences and reduces training costs by 34% (in GPU-days) compared to the state-of-the-art Pairformer backbone used in AlphaFold3-style models like Boltz-1.

Strong Empirical Results: The model maintains highly competitive performance across a wide range of standard biomolecular cofolding benchmarks, including RCSB, CASP15, PoseBusters (protein-ligand), antibody-antigen, and protein-nucleic acid complexes.

Validation in Downstream Applications: The integration into BoltzDesign (named BindFast) clearly demonstrates the practical utility of the simplified architecture. It offers a 2x speedup in sequence optimization and allows the design of 30% longer sequences on an 80GB A100 GPU without running out of memory.

Thorough Analysis and Ablations: The paper does an excellent job of isolating the contributions of different modules. The use of distogram evaluation, recycling step sensitivity, and dropout-based sparsity analyses (low-norm vs. random dropout) provides deep insights into why the architecture works so well.
weaknesses: Incremental Architectural Novelty: The individual components (triangle multiplication, FFN, and diffusion modules) are already widely known and used in the literature (e.g., AlphaFold3, Boltz-1). The main contribution lies in identifying which modules can be safely discarded rather than inventing a new primitive.

Slight Performance Drops on Specific Metrics: Although highly competitive, Pairmixer occasionally lags slightly behind the full Pairformer model on certain complex metrics, such as DockQ for protein-protein interfaces.

Role of the Diffusion Module in Sequence Processing: Because the sequence updates are completely bypassed in the Pairmixer backbone (passing s_init directly to s_backbone), the downstream Diffusion Module likely carries a larger burden of sequence-wise feature extraction. A more detailed discussion or ablation on how the diffusion module's capacity offsets the backbone's simplification would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Strong and highly practical motivation: Bypassing the computational bottleneck of triangle attention in AlphaFold3-style backbones is critical for high-throughput screening and structural biology applications.

Convincing empirical results: The authors train multiple model sizes (up to Large) of their proposed Pairmixer architecture on top of Boltz-1 from scratch, showing it matches the state-of-the-art Pairformer backbone across PDB, CASP15, and PoseBusters benchmarks.
Significant efficiency gains: Delivers up to 4x faster inference on long sequences and reduces training time by 34% (GPU-days) across multiple model sizes.

Strong downstream validation: Successfully demonstrates the utility of Pairmixer in hallucination-based binder design (BindFast), achieving over 2x speedups and expanding target sequence size limits by 30% before out-of-memory (OOM) errors.

Thorough analysis and ablation studies: Includes distogram performance evaluations, Match3 synthetic task evaluations to isolate 3-way interactions, and sensitivity analyses on recycling steps and hidden dimensions.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is somewhat limited, as the paper primarily simplifies the existing AlphaFold3/Pairformer architecture by removing components (triangle attention, sequence updates) rather than introducing entirely new architectural primitives.
There are minor performance regressions on specific complex/docking benchmarks (e.g., DockQ scores on CASP15 and PoseBusters), which might be relevant for highly sensitive downstream applications.
The model does not train a confidence model (as noted in Figure 6), which makes practical deployment slightly less convenient since predictions cannot be ranked natively.
